_comment: One rule, two languages. Run by BOTH frontend/src/components/transactions/mergeEligibility.test.ts and backend/tests/unit/test_merge_offer.py. A rule changed on one side only fails on the other.
_why: The client's copy of this rule had already drifted. It knew about accounts, reconciled pairs, splits and transfer legs, but not about bank identity — so the register offered Merge on two SimpleFIN rows carrying different bank ids, the server refused every save, and the modal swallowed the refusal. A real duplicate of a reconciled Hobby Lobby row could not be merged and the UI would not say why.
_shape: `server_accepts` is domain/merging.may_offer_merge — would the merge go through with no survivor requested. `register_offers` is whether the register draws the Merge button. Two invariants, both tested on both sides: the register never offers what the server refuses, and where it offers LESS the divergence is named below. Which row survives stays a server decision (choose_survivor); offerability is not survivorship. `kept` (on every case the register offers) is the side the server keeps whatever the user picks — choose_survivor's reconciled and structured rules — or null where the choice is the user's. The merge preview locks its Keep badge from the same rule (mergeEligibility.lockedSurvivor), so this pins that copy too.
_deliberate_divergence: The register does not offer a merge involving a transfer leg, though the server accepts three shapes of one: the leg survives and the plain duplicate goes; a reconciled plain row survives and takes the transfer over (the leg's partner is relinked to it); and two legs merge, which merges their partners on the other account in the same change. The preview modal shows two rows becoming one; it cannot show a partner being relinked or a second pair being merged in another account, and the register does not hold the partner rows the third shape is decided on (`partners`, which only the server suite reads). A merge the user cannot see the consequences of is not one the register should offer, and the duplicate-review queue, which is where transfer duplicates arrive, accepts all three. Splits used to be held back the same way; the preview now says where a split's lines go, so they are offered. Bounded here, and pinned by the containment test — if the gap widens, both suites fail.
_partners: `partners` (server suite only) maps a leg's `transfer_id` key to its partner row; a partner's `transfer_id` names the side it belongs to. Amounts default to -500.00 on `a`/`b` — a $500 card payment out of checking.

cases.note: the ordinary duplicate: one hand-entered, one from the bank
a reconciled row may absorb a duplicate — it survives, and that is the point
two bank rows sharing one bank id are the same record seen twice
one bank row, one hand-entered row, both reconciled: neither may go
the Hobby Lobby case: two SimpleFIN rows, two different bank ids. The server has always refused this; the register offered it anyway
different bank ids, neither reconciled — still two distinct bank records
both reconciled: the statement vouched for both, so neither may go
different accounts: a merge would move money between them
a split and a plain duplicate: the split is kept and the plain row merges into it
a reconciled bank row and the receipt split typed before it: the bank row is kept and takes the split's lines. This used to be refused, and the user was told to unreconcile
a reconciled split and an unreconciled split: one would be merged away into the other's lines
deliberate divergence: same, for a transfer leg — the server keeps the leg, the register will not show what becomes of its partner

deliberate divergence: a reconciled bank row and the card payment typed as a transfer before it — the bank row is kept and takes the transfer over. This used to be refused with 'Cannot merge away a transfer'
deliberate divergence: two transfers for one card payment — the typed one, and the bank's two rows a sync paired — merge on both accounts. This used to be refused with 'Cannot merge away a transfer'
two transfers whose card legs are for different amounts: the other account's two legs don't match, so neither pair is merged
two transfers whose card legs are both reconciled: neither card leg may go, so neither pair is merged
a split line: act on its parent instead — refused by both
two splits: the loser would be merged away whichever survives
